claims.text: Integrating an active-learning-trained machine-learning potential into nested thermodynamic integration will substantially reduce the cost of evaluating fusion free energies and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The ML-augmented nested thermodynamic integration method will retain ab initio levels of fidelity.
The proposed method is intended to cover elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy systems in both solid and liquid phases near their fusion points.
Most explicit ab initio molecular dynamics can be replaced by an ML potential trained on a minimal set of actively selected ab initio snapshots.
The ML potential can be used within nested thermodynamic integration while retaining anharmonic effects.
The ML-augmented integration can retain vibrational-entropy contributions.
The ML-augmented integration can retain electron-vibration coupling effects.
Vibrational anharmonicity and electron-vibration coupling are significant in the targeted temperature regimes near melting.
A neural-network or Gaussian-approximation potential trained on targeted ab initio MD snapshots can learn the relevant local free-energy landscape.
The trained interatomic potential can correctly capture anharmonic effects.
Active learning will efficiently identify and sample the relevant regions of the free-energy surface.
Using the ML surrogate for thermodynamic integration will make free-energy evaluation faster.
Periodic reweighting or corrections based on sparse ab initio data will maintain the accuracy needed for entropy and electron-vibration effects.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by approximately 50–100 times relative to full explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
Fusion free energies will be predicted within approximately 5% of explicit ab initio benchmarks.
Melting temperatures will be predicted within approximately 5% of explicit ab initio benchmarks.
For binary systems, the method's fidelity will be at least comparable to TOR-TILD.
The proposed method will make free-energy calculations feasible for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The method is validated near melting for elemental and binary systems.
Accuracy in highly complex multicomponent systems may be limited by sparse training data, extreme anharmonicity, complex electron-vibration coupling, or rare configurations near phase boundaries.
